answers.answer: A collection of independent Godot Engine demonstration projects: each project.godot directory is a runnable demo, not one repository-wide game. It is hosted by the godotengine organization; the license credits Godot Engine contributors, and individual demos are linked under the Godot Foundation publisher. Users run/import demos through Godot's project manager; most also have browser exports. Individual maintainers are not established here.

Repository level: independent demo directories, import/version guidance, contribution guidance, and licensing. Pong is one 2D example, not the repository's central application. Its project.godot configures startup/input/rendering; pong.tscn assembles the scene; ball.gd moves/resets the ball; paddle.gd handles movement and rebounds; wall.gd resets out-of-bounds balls; ceiling_floor.gd adjusts vertical rebounds. Textures and collision shapes supply presentation/contact geometry.

The repository boundary is per project.godot directory. Verified languages include GDScript in 2d/pong and C# in the separate mono/pong demo; this is not an exhaustive repository language inventory. Selected Pong uses Godot 4.7 features, Compatibility rendering, .gd scripts, a .tscn scene/resource graph, Area2D nodes and signals, and project-defined Input actions. res:// paths resolve within that Pong project.

2d/pong/project.godot sets run/main_scene to res://pong.tscn. Godot instantiates its Pong Node2D scene and attached scripts. Ball's @onready captures its initial position; its _process(delta) advances it. Paddles initialize action names in _ready() and poll movement in _process(). These are engine lifecycle callbacks, not a repository-wide main() function.

The trigger is 2d/pong/logic/wall.gd::_on_wall_area_entered(area): if area.name is Ball, call area.reset(). The implementation is logic/ball.gd::reset(): restore Vector2.LEFT, the position saved by @onready, and DEFAULT_SPEED (100.0). Both side walls are wired to that handler in pong.tscn.

pong.tscn binds four scripts: paddle.gd to Left/Right, ball.gd to Ball, wall.gd to LeftWall/RightWall, and ceiling_floor.gd to Ceiling/Floor. It uses paddle.png, ball.png, separator.png; four RectangleShape2D resources; ColorRect background, Sprite2D children/separator, CollisionShape2D children, and Camera2D. Six area_entered connections bind paddles, side walls, ceiling and floor to their local handlers.

Godot overlap detection emits a side wall's area_entered signal; the scene routes it to that wall's _on_wall_area_entered. The handler checks the incoming Area2D's name and invokes area.reset(); the scene's Ball node has ball.gd, whose reset restores direction/position/speed. Dynamic boundary: engine signal delivery and runtime receiver dispatch; the parameter is Area2D and identity is a name check, not a statically typed Ball reference. No runtime collision execution was performed.

The evidenced direct call consumer is wall.gd::_on_wall_area_entered via area.reset(). Both LeftWall and RightWall use it through scene bindings. Changing reset semantics therefore changes their out-of-bounds response. This establishes the selected scene's consumer, not an exhaustive repository-wide caller inventory.

The documented example is 2d/pong, titled Pong with GDScript. Its README explains that contact between ball, walls and paddles emits signals modifying the ball. Import/run this project: project.godot selects pong.tscn, whose side-wall connections enter wall.gd and then ball.gd::reset(). This is a documented runnable example with a source-supported reset path, not evidence of an automated reset test.

project.godot defines left/right_move_up/down actions with keyboard and joypad events. paddle.gd::_ready lowercases the node name (Left/Right) and constructs those action names. Each _process(delta) subtracts up strength from down strength, multiplies by MOVE_SPEED (100) and delta, adds to position.y, then clamps to [16, viewport height - 16]. Input enters through Godot's action system; device event delivery is engine-managed.
